# Background

For paid open access, the dominant model is that article processing charges (APCs) are invoiced to the institution of the corresponding author. However, corresponding-author data has often been unavailable as open research information. Some studies therefore used first author affiliation data as a proxy. This poster tests the policy assumption against real payment data. 

# Data

![](images/flowchart.png){fig-align="center"}

# How complete is the coverage of OpenAlex corresponding-author data?

Corresponding-author data in OpenAlex is the basis for testing the policy assumption that APCs are invoiced to that author's institution. We computed the share of corresponding-author data for the entire dataset and broken down by publication year.

:::: {layout-ncol="2"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center


article_level |> 
  count(has_corr) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = has_corr, y = n, fill = has_corr)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 5.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.17))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#051740", "FALSE" = "#4086e0"), guide = "none") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  labs(x = "has corresponding author", y = "number of articles")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center

article_level |>
  count(period, has_corr) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(period), y = n, fill = has_corr)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.9)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.9),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 4.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.17))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#051740", "FALSE" = "#4086e0"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "TRUE", "FALSE" = "FALSE")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  labs(x = "publication year", y = "number of articles", fill = "has \ncorresponding")
```

```{=typst}
#align(center)[
  #text(size: 18pt, style: "italic")[

  ]
]
```

```{=typst}
#align(center)[
```

::::

Coverage is high in general and also proves stable across 2021–2024, but drops in 2025. This might be due to a lag
in OpenAPC data submission and enrichment rather than a change in coverage in OpenAlex.

# How well does ROR-based matching work?

Matching the paying institution's ROR ID to author affiliations works well overall and ROR relationships meaningfully extend what exact ID matching alone would find.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

shares <- article_level |>
  summarise(
    n_articles  = n(),
    exact       = sum(exact_any),
    rel         = sum(payer_any & !exact_any),
    none        = sum(!payer_any),
    exact_share = mean(exact_any),
    rel_share   = mean(payer_any & !exact_any),
    none_share  = mean(!payer_any)
  )

```

```{=typst}
#let value_box(value, n, label, color: rgb("#051740")) = {
  box(
    width: 100%,
    stroke: none,
    align(center)[
      #text(size: 32pt, weight: "bold", fill: color)[#value]
      #v(1pt)
      #text(size: 22pt, fill: rgb("#4086e0"))[n = #n]
      #v(4pt)
      #text(size: 22pt, fill: rgb("#444444"))[#label]
    ]
  )
}

#grid(
  columns: (1fr, 1fr, 1fr),
  gutter: 1em,
  value_box("`r scales::percent(shares$exact_share, accuracy = 1)`", "`r format(shares$exact, big.mark = ",")`", "exact ROR match"),
  value_box("`r scales::percent(shares$rel_share, accuracy = 1)`", "`r format(shares$rel, big.mark = ",")`", "only via ROR relationships"),
  value_box("`r scales::percent(shares$none_share, accuracy = 1)`", "`r format(shares$none, big.mark = ",")`", "no match"),
  )
```

Breaking down the 7% matched only via relationships by relationship type shows that most affiliations are matched via the related relationship, followed by the child relationship. 

```{=typst}
#grid(
  columns: (1fr, 1fr, 1fr, 1fr),
  gutter: 1em,
  value_box("`r scales::percent(rel_shares$share_of_articles[1], accuracy = 0.01)`", "`r format(rel_shares$n_articles[1], big.mark = ",")`", "child"),
    value_box("`r scales::percent(rel_shares$share_of_articles[2], accuracy = 0.01)`", "`r format(rel_shares$n_articles[2], big.mark = ",")`", "parent"),
      value_box("`r scales::percent(rel_shares$share_of_articles[3], accuracy = 0.01)`", "`r format(rel_shares$n_articles[3], big.mark = ",")`", "predecessor"),
  value_box("`r scales::percent(rel_shares$share_of_articles[4], accuracy = 0.01)`", "`r format(rel_shares$n_articles[4], big.mark = ",")`", "related"),      
  )
```

*Note that relationships might differ for separate affiliations of co-authors leading to an article potentially having multiple relationship matches.*

Breaking down the 6% unmatched articles by reason shows that most unmatched cases stem from affiliations either genuinely having no connection to the paying institution or from gaps in recording multi-level institutional relationships in ROR.


```{=typst}

    value_box("`r scales::percent(reason$share_of_no_match[2], accuracy = 0.01)`", "`r format(reason$n[2], big.mark = ",")`", "no author affiliation has a ROR ID"),
      value_box("`r scales::percent(reason$share_of_no_match[3], accuracy = 0.01)`", "`r format(reason$n[3], big.mark = ",")`", "payer ROR record has no \n relationships recorded"),
  )
```

# At which author-position is the paying institution recorded as affiliation?

Categorizing the paying institutions by author-position combinations shows they are most often affiliated with the first, last, *and*
corresponding author simultaneously.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-align: center

article_level |> 
  count(has_corr, position_category) |> 
  group_by(has_corr) |> 
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = fct_reorder(position_category, share, .fun = max), fill = has_corr)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.9)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.9),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 5.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "TRUE"    = "#051740",
    "FALSE" = "#4086e0"
  )) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  labs(x = "share of articles", y = NULL, fill = "has corresponding")
```

```{=typst}
#align(center)[
  #text(size: 18pt, style: "italic")[
    Figure 3: Share of articles per author-position category, with and without corresponding-author data
  ]
]
```


Without corresponding-author data, first-author affiliation identifies the paying institution for the large majority of articles. For articles with corresponding-author data, corresponding author affiliations show the highest recall for identifying the paying institution.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false


payer <- article_level |> 
  group_by(has_corr) |> 
  summarise(
    n_articles      = n(),
    payer_at_first  = mean(payer_first),
    payer_at_last   = mean(payer_last),
    payer_at_middle = mean(payer_middle),
    payer_at_corr   = mean(payer_corr),
    no_match        = mean(!payer_any)
  )
```

# Are first author affiliations a good proxy for identifying the paying institution?

Across all articles, first- and corresponding-author affiliations identify largely the same set of articles. Using first-author affiliations as a fallback or an additional filter captures articles that corresponding-author data alone would miss. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

venn_list <- list(
  "Corresponding" = article_level |> 
    filter(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "last + corresponding", "middle + corresponding"
    )) |> 
    pull(doi_norm),
  "First" = article_level |> 
    filter(position_category %in% c(
      "first + last + corresponding", "first + corresponding",
      "first + last", "first only"
    )) |> 
    pull(doi_norm)
)
```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: center

ggVennDiagram(venn_list, label = "both", set_size = 6, label_size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#cbd8e8", high = "#051740") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 0.75)
```

```{=typst}
#align(center)[
  #text(size: 18pt, style: "italic")[
    Figure 4: Overlap between articles matched via first and corresponding author
  ]
]
```

# Conclusion

- **Coverage:** OpenAlex provides corresponding-author data for the large majority of articles.
- **Matching:** ROR-based matching identifies the paying institution for most articles, ROR relationships extend exact ID matching.
- **Author position:** The paying institution is most often affiliated with the first, last, *and* corresponding author.
- **First author as proxy:** First-author affiliation can serve as a fallback or an additional filter.
